Messages.Author: Andrew S. Davidson
Messages.Body:
I played the antitribu Malkavians in the Clan War at Gencon UK. I
quite enjoyed the event though my Malkavian Games were handicapped by
the banning of the Monocle of Clarity and I lost more than I won. The
high point was ousting James "Legbiter" McLellan which he deserved for
keeping us kicking our heels while he went in search of more money.

Following recent discussions, I was naturally interested in the
shuffling procedure. I didn't see any mana-weaving here (the French
Shadowfist players were another matter). I elected to shuffle my
prey's deck each time but didn't see anyone else do this.

There was no problem with James. His deck was unsleeved and a couple
of quick riffles passed without comment. In the second game, my
prey's deck was encased in black Ultra-Pro sleeves. These were quite
sticky but I was able to corner-riffle these fairly well. My
grand-prey grumbled that I was bending the cards and that my prey
could insist that I shuffle so as not to damage the cards, i.e. by
overhand shuffling. I told him that he was wrong and did a third
riffle for good measure.

I forget exactly what happened in the third game - another sleeved
deck I think. My main memory of that was the odd behaviour of my
grand-prey. When an early bleed was deflected into him, he put me in
a Trap. This didn't seem very friendly or sensible so I put his big
bruiser into a Coma. This did neither of us much good but at least I
lasted longer than he did. I still stood a chance until my prey kept
walking into my predator's deflections - these seemed annoyingly
predictable to me. My prey in game 2 seemed fairly clueless too. I
start to understand what Matt Green is complaining about - are there a
lot of rabbits in the UK scene?

I dressed as an escaped mental patient for the event and talked Dave
into giving me a small spot prize of a booster for the best costume.
James' sinister dark glasses and lightweight suit looked the part too
- just right for the Giovanni.

Thanks to Dave for running the event. Let's hope that Bloodlines
creates some more clans so that there will be even more players for
the next one.

Andrew

On Tue, 4 Sep 2001 18:57:05 +0100, Rob Treasure wrote:

>Bending cards ? not fine.

>I spoke to a few players on Saturday who were understandably pissed at
>having their cards bent on Friday. I agree that a damn good shuffle or cut
>is in order before everyone starts, but shuffling the decks corner style 3,
>4, 5 times is a bit much don't you think ?

It's nothing. WotC usually used good card stock for their cards. One
test of a counterfeit Magic card was to bend it so that the top
touched the bottom. It shouldn't crease when you do this and should
have enough "snap" to easily flatten out again. The cards are made in
this way precisely so that you can riffle-shuffle them - it's
expected. If you put them in heavy sleeves then they are nearly
indestructible. Even if they are not, this is just too bad -
shuffling is a mandatory part of the game.

I've just tested a WW card from SW - bent it double and it went back
fine.

>What about the factor 6 or 8 method where you deal a deck into 6 or 8 face
>down piles to shuffle? I wouldn't mind this *IF* you asked me early enough
>and didn't delay the game. Again this would seem a little anal to me, but
>whatever fills your bag and all that :o)

Pile-shuffling is commonly used in Shadowfist where it's the easiest
method of dealing with the large (100+) decks of sleeved cards you
often get there. But it's not random and so can't be relied on as a
proper shuffle.

>Part of the appeal of VTES for me is the fact that (rightly or wrongly) the
>level of honourable and trustworthy opponents you come across is a lot
>higher than certain other card games. I know that decks can be stacked,
>cards rigged etc. but if a player is determined to cheat, shuffling their
>cards (especially in this less than respectable way) ain't gonna stop them.

I saw someone blatantly stacking their deck at the last VTES
tournament I played in (at Watford). My impression is that VTES has a
similar ethos to Magic because of its common heritage and I am
therefore not inclined to trust anyone - cheating is certainly
commonplace in Magic.

>If I can see players shuffling their decks before starting I'm usually
>happy.

Me too. I was just putting the VEKN rules to the test.

>Could you not play on Saturday? I was looking forward to a few rounds with
>you.

I was running another event that afternoon and then playing in another
event in the evening. In any case, the ordinary UK event seems too
political for my taste. If I'm going to play that sort of game, I'd
rather play the Survivor CCG which is comparatively fast, clean and
simple. There you decide who to throw to the sharks without all the
fiddly mechanics of VTES. Amounts to much the same thing - I expect
you'd be good at it too.

Andrew

Messages.Author: Frederick Scott
Messages.Body:
"Andrew S. Davidson" wrote:
> Pile-shuffling is commonly used in Shadowfist where it's the easiest
> method of dealing with the large (100+) decks of sleeved cards you
> often get there. But it's not random and so can't be relied on as a
> proper shuffle.

I strongly disagree. Pile shuffling *alone* is not very random. You
simply reorder the original set of cards into some new set/predictable
order. However, think in terms of a pile shuffle, followed by a few
random cuts, followed by another pile shuffle. The ultimately result
will differ immensely and quite unpredictable based on the exact spot
of each of the intervening cuts. Pile shuffle then cut at card numbers
22 and 57, then pile shuffle again, then cut at card #45 then pile shuffle
a third time will differ a great deal than if the cuts were made at card
number 23, 58, and 46 respectively. A slight variance in pile shuffles
goes a long way in randomness.

Fred

On Fri, 07 Sep 2001 09:12:05 +0100, Andy Brown wrote:

>Last year I went to a Magic tournement where one of my oppenents riffle

>whenever I went searching my library. He was quite forceful about it,
>and I am glad that I had them in Deck Protectors. His cards were not,
>and you could see the edges wearing somewhat.

There are many CCG players who don't use sleeves. One reason for this
is so that they can riffle shuffle their own decks easily. This is
the normal state of affairs in a card game. The use of sleeves is a
somewhat bizarre introduction to card gaming, caused by the collecting
aspect. I am surprised to find that Vampire players are especially
prissy about this as the cards are fairly cheap and not especially
collectable.

>I personally only cut a someones deck, never do a further shuffle,
>although it is within the rules to do so. I think it may be courteous
>to ask before riffle shuffling someones deck, as otherwise it may
>offend, and, when it does happen, cause the edges of the cards to wear.

A unsleeved card will suffer all sorts of wear and tear - just
touching the cards with sweaty, dirty hands will do more damage than I
care for myself.

If you don't want your cards damaged by shuffling then use hard
sleeves. If you want to keep them in Mint condition then don't play
with them at all - keep them in a binder. Non volenti fit injuria.

Andrew

>somewhat bizarre introduction to card gaming, caused by the collecting
>aspect. I am surprised to find that Vampire players are especially
>prissy about this as the cards are fairly cheap and not especially
>collectable.

Because of the NL aspect of the game, for one thing. In <X>, if you
have 4 copies of a card, any spares are fine. In Jyhad, if you have 6
copies of a card, all of them are potentially playable in a deck, rather
than 2 being marked up as "spare".

There's also a marked demographic shift between V:TES and most other
games, which may account for some changes. Magic is generally younger
than V:TES. Perhaps the older V:TES population attributes more care to
things. (Parallels with say parents vs children and their attitudes
towards their belongings.)

A lot of people also just like the cards. Sure, I can replace them but
some of them are quite pretty. I know I've had numerous conversations
with people over the years about such-and-such card being really cute,
or liking what the artist did on this card with the eyes, or whatever.

Laugh out loud funny.
Almost every card ever printed for Jyhad/V:tES is legal for
play, and a great many of them (perhaps even a majority)
are currently out of print, some probably forever.
There are a great number of the game pieces for this
game that cannot be acquired for less than $5 per, and
many more which are not available by any reasonable
definition. And if you think over $100 retail for a
box of cards is "fairly cheap," then you've lost perspective
on what "fairly cheap" means in any rational definition
of game prices. And finally, since worn cards can be
ruled as marked cards at the discretion of a tournament
judge, or since you can be declared a cheater and disqualified
because the only Conditionings you own happen to be Jyhad-
backed, sleeves can become quite a priority if you wish to
compete with a minimum of random interference.

- Jason Bell

Messages.Author: Andrew S. Davidson
Messages.Body:
On 9 Sep 2001 06:08:57 -0700, Simidh wrote:

>I am all for the cards being random but surely that can be achieved by a
>series of cuts, overhand shuffles

These are much slower than a riffle shuffle for the same amount of
randomisation. It takes about 2000 overhand shuffles to properly
shuffle a 52 card deck and presumably many more for a 90-card VTES
deck.

>and a face down spread of the cards via a random number?

Something of this sort is probably the most random method but I have
never seen it done. As with overhand shuffling, it's not practical
within the time allowed.

>I like to take good care of my cards without them having
>worn corners or having them bent.

If your cards are in good sleeves then you have little to worry about.
I routinely riffle shuffle my own decks and my cards are fine.

BTW, I was at a Doomtown tournament at the Card Mart today and one of
the players asked if I'd read about the shuffling controversy. I was
surprised that he'd heard of this thread but it turned out that he was
talking about a similar fuss on the Warlord list. This crops up so
often that it needs to be drummed into folk that stacking your deck is
cheating. In the VTES context, what is the penalty for a player
presenting his deck to his predator for shuffling when it has not been
sufficiently randomised? Loss of game? Would the predator get a VP
for this?

Andrew

The cards are so cheap that I don't put them into sleeves straight
away. That's when they are most at risk - when they are not in decks.
When I opened the box before Gencon UK I dropped a big stack of the
cards on the floor but just blew the dust off them and put them back -
they are still in good shape. They'll pick up more damage when
they're in my card boxes though - being handled when I'm deck
building. The worst thing is dinging the edges with my fingernails
when I'm sorting through them. It's not a real problem though -
they're still perfectly playable and, short of an act of God, will
last longer than I do.

Let's get a sense of perspective here - what really matters is looking
after our own minds and bodies, not keeping some pasteboard looking
good. I'm quite horrified that smoking is allowed at any VEKN event.
If mobile phones are forbidden and players are allowed to call judges
to shuffle their precious decks then let's protect our lungs too.

Andrew

"Jason Bell" <Jason...@mail.com> wrote in news:0UYm7.258071$J37.68437658
@typhoon.southeast.rr.com:

Without detracting from the benefits of sleeves any; how have you managed
to produce any overplayed/overworn rares? Many of my cards show a slight
bit of 'edge wear', and it's quite amusing to put some of my Bum's Rush
next to, say, my Fortitude to see the difference, but it hardly reduces the
playability in the slightest.

Oh, and I riffle-shuffle my cards lots (for everyone else out there). I
get more "bend" in my cards from just having the damn things stored in a
box in Georgia's humidity. But seriously, these are NOT the crown jewels.
They're a game. They're meant to be played with, touched, and eventually,
yes, to wear out. If you want to collect, get a binder, put one of each in
for your collection, and play with the rest.

> I don't know the exact calculus used to determine how card back
> organization can lead to a ruling of marked cards, I assume that

In a library with mixed-back vampire/jyhad cards, there is a 60-40 rule
that used to apply and I'm assuming still does -- no more than 60% of your
library can be of one card-back type. I've come up against this since I
began playing tournament V:TES and including DS/AH/Sabbat vampires, since
all of my original cards were Jyhad-backed. All three of my D*C tourney
decks were compliant with the 60/40 rule, which is pretty damned tricky in
a Cryptic Mission/Burst of Sunlight/Weather Control deck. Thank god I had
a pile of Sabbat CMs.

Even if you come under the official rule, it is still possible to "mark"
cards by including, say, nothing but Jyhad bleed and Vampire stealth. I
usually make sure I have a few of each in any given "category", so that
anyone wishing to make that complain can be shown that I really have -no-
idea what's coming up next. This is as close as it ever gets to a
judgement call.

> it too is a judgement call, so again I'm better off behind sleeves.

While the 60/40 rule applies to one's crypt, too, I routinely sleeve my
crypts. Partly, it provides convenient separation when i'm using my clear
plastic deck-boxes (they hold two decks each), and partly, it has to do
with your below statement...

> The next crypt vampire is Vampire and not Jyhad, so I am assured
> that it is not Camille. Does that give me enough information to have
> gained an unfair advantage? I don't know, but I don't want to
> have to find out the unpleasant way.

Yes, it DOES give you enough information, although the only time the top of
your crypt matters is when you're considering spending a pool to go looking
for a vampire. The transfers are irrelevant, but the pool is not; anything
you can learn about that vampire will help you, because it's much easier to
remember what 12 vampires are in your crypt than what 80 cards are in your
library. And if that decision helps you decide whether or not to spend a
pool, ... well, one pool matters. =)

--
Derek
